lesson.title: A Thousand Miles of Grief: The Cherokee Forced March West
lesson.summary: In 1838 and 1839, federal troops forcibly marched roughly sixteen thousand Cherokee people to Indian Territory under brutal conditions that killed an estimated four thousand along the way.
lesson.body:
The Trail of Tears refers most specifically to the forced removal of the Cherokee Nation from its homeland in the Southeast to Indian Territory west of the Mississippi River, carried out mainly in 1838 and 1839 under the authority granted by the Indian Removal Act of 1830. It stands as one of the most devastating episodes of the era, a direct human consequence of the removal policy Andrew Jackson had championed, even though the worst of the Cherokee removal took place after Jackson left office in 1837, during the presidency of his chosen successor, Martin Van Buren.

The removal followed the disputed Treaty of New Echota, signed in 1835 by a small faction of Cherokee leaders known as the Treaty Party, including Major Ridge, his son John Ridge, and Elias Boudinot, who believed removal was inevitable and negotiated for the best terms they could get. The treaty ceded all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi in exchange for land in Indian Territory and payment, but it was never approved by Principal Chief John Ross or by the vast majority of the Cherokee people, who considered it illegitimate. Ross led a delegation to Washington to protest and gathered thousands of signatures against the treaty, but the federal government treated it as binding.

When the Cherokee did not leave voluntarily by the treaty's deadline in May 1838, President Van Buren ordered General Winfield Scott to enforce removal with federal troops and state militia. Soldiers rounded up roughly sixteen thousand Cherokee men, women, and children, often with little warning, forced them into hastily built stockades, and then marched or transported them roughly a thousand miles west over the following months. Conditions along the route were brutal, marked by inadequate food, exposure to harsh weather including a severe winter, and outbreaks of disease. Historians commonly estimate that around four thousand Cherokee died during the roundup, in the internment camps, or along the journey itself, though precise figures are difficult to establish and some estimates differ.

Although the phrase Trail of Tears is most closely associated with the Cherokee removal, similar forced marches struck the Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, and Seminole nations during the same broad period, part of the same removal policy set in motion by the Indian Removal Act. The Seminole in Florida resisted removal militarily in a prolonged conflict known as the Second Seminole War, which dragged on for years and cost the United States far more in money and lives than officials had expected.

The Trail of Tears permanently uprooted Native nations that had lived in the Southeast for centuries, destroying homes, farms, and sacred sites built up over generations of Indigenous life in the region, and forcing survivors to rebuild their societies in unfamiliar territory in what is now Oklahoma. The Cherokee Nation, the Choctaw Nation, and the other removed tribes reestablished governments and communities there, communities that continue today, but the removal remains one of the clearest examples in American history of a democratically popular policy inflicting catastrophic harm on a population excluded from that democracy altogether.
